Puissant

PWEE-sunt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Puissant is having great, commanding power — a formal, old-fashioned word for strength on a grand, almost legendary scale.

Diplomats spoke carefully around the puissant trade alliance, wary of provoking a partnership that controlled half the region's shipping lanes.

Worked Example

Even neighboring kingdoms that despised the queen admitted, quietly, that her navy was the most puissant fleet on the sea.

Puissant is a formal, almost old-fashioned word for powerful -- you'll meet it most often in stories about kings, armies, and nations.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mighty: Mighty is the everyday word for having great strength or power — a mighty river, a mighty blow. Puissant means much the same thing but lives in a different register: a deliberately formal, old-fashioned word met in legends and histories, not daily speech.

formidable: Formidable describes power as felt by whoever has to face it — a formidable opponent inspires dread and respect. Puissant describes the might itself, grandly and from a distance, without saying that anyone in particular is afraid of it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

powerless: having no power or strength

feeble: weak; lacking strength

Where it sits · how commanding the power is — strong → puissant → invincible

strong vs. puissant: Strong just describes physical or general power -- it doesn't carry puissant's sense of commanding, almost legendary might.

invincible vs. puissant: Invincible goes beyond even puissant: a puissant army can still be beaten by a greater one, but an invincible force can never be defeated at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — puiss

Root — puiss: to be able, powerful (from Old French puissant, from Latin posse, 'to be able')

Suffix — -ant

Suffix — -ant: having the quality of; being (Latin -antem)

Put it together

Put it together: Puissant combines puiss ('to be able, powerful' -- Old French, from Latin posse, 'to be able') with -ant ('having the quality of') -- literally 'being able,' which came to mean powerful or mighty.

Use the root in a new word: possible

Use the root in a new word: possible: The word possible comes from that same Latin root posse -- something possible is, quite literally, 'able to be.'

Word Choice

Puissant is a deliberately old-fashioned, literary word -- you'll find it in fantasy novels and historical fiction far more often than in everyday speech, where 'powerful' or 'mighty' would sound more natural.
